```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(tinytable)
})
curve <- read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- read_csv("../data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(curve == "positive")
menu <- read_csv("../data/menu_options.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
periods <- read_csv("../data/display_periods.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
loo <- read_csv("../data/display_loo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bailout <- read_csv("../data/display_bailout.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cnames <- read_csv("../data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(cntry, country)

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign; pct() takes values already in per cent and
# rounds halves up, as the specification menu does, so that the pages agree
num <- \(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
minus <- \(x) gsub("-", "−", format(x), fixed = TRUE)

# shares of a set of curve rows below zero, and below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05
below <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports)
below_sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports & d$sig)
fk <- \(ax, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == ax]
dv <- \(ax, op, col) devs[[col]][devs$axis == ax & devs$option == op & devs$rule == "wcr_rademacher"]
ref <- curve |> filter(is_reference)
twoway <- curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway")
country <- curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_country")

# the displays of section 8: the reproduced specification and its country twin
is_ref_spec <- \(d) d$outcome == "mcosmo" & d$predictor == "unemp" & d$copredictor == "none" &
  d$pred_form == "raw"
per_ref <- \(smp, col) periods[[col]][is_ref_spec(periods) & periods$estimator == "fe_twoway" &
                                        periods$sample == smp]
per_unemp <- periods |> filter(predictor == "unemp")
loo_two <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway", left_out != "none")
loo_cty <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_country", left_out != "none")
vs <- \(cc) loo_two$variation_share[loo_two$left_out == cc]
ba <- \(grp, col) bailout[[col]][bailout$outcome == "mcosmo" & bailout$predictor == "unemp" &
                                   bailout$estimator == "fe_twoway" & bailout$group == grp]
design_label <- c(fe_twoway = "Two-way fixed effects", fe_country = "Country fixed effects")
```

This is the multiverse module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is optional. The course teaches you to *run* a multiverse analysis: fix one specification in a preregistration, run it, and read your result against the `r nrow(curve)` specifications of the curve of the claim. This module is about where the idea came from, what it is claimed to do, and the arguments that are now being made against it. It is a companion to [the inference reading](../exercise/reading-inference.qmd), which covers one narrow question, namely what a curve-level test can and cannot establish. The question here is broader. The method you practised on the workshop day is under live debate in 2025–26, the objections raised against it are strong ones, and the aim of this module is that you can take a position in that debate. Throughout, the course materials serve as the worked example, sometimes as an answer to a criticism and sometimes as a case to which the criticism applies.

## 1. Origins {#sec-origins}

The founding statement is a 2016 paper by Sara Steegen, Francis Tuerlinckx, Andrew Gelman and Wolf Vanpaemel [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse]. Their starting point is the construction of the data, before any model is fitted: turning raw data into an analysable dataset involves choices – which respondents to exclude, how to code a variable, where to cut a scale – and several options are usually reasonable. Instead of privileging one arbitrarily assembled dataset, they propose constructing every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and running the analysis on all of them, so that the reader sees how much the conclusion owes to decisions nobody would defend as the uniquely correct ones. The idea connects directly to Gelman and Loken's 'garden of forking paths' [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]. A researcher who makes each choice once, on the fly, has walked one path through a branching garden, and the single p-value at the end contains no record of the branches. The closing sentence of the 2016 paper sets the ambition plainly: "it should become standard practice to go beyond a single data set analysis and to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results", followed immediately by a concession that the critics would later press hard on – "performing a multiverse analysis will often be difficult, and to a large extent subjective" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710].

Two things about the original paper matter for everything that follows. First, its multiverse was *customised for critique*: the alternative datasets were choices that the original authors of the target study "might themselves have considered", drawn from their own prior publications. It was therefore a post-mortem on the flexibility of one team, not a general survey of the ways in which the question could be answered, and the distinction matters again in section 2. Second, Steegen and colleagues already foresaw the extension that the course curve puts into practice: alongside the data multiverse they sketch a *model* multiverse, in which "One specific analysis thus corresponds to a single sample from a model multiverse" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710]. They also place the whole idea in an older lineage running through perturbation and sensitivity analysis in economics and Bayesian statistics, and what the 2016 paper added to that lineage was the demand that the whole distribution of results be shown.

The modelling side of the idea was developed separately as **specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis], which enumerates the defensible ways of specifying the test, estimates all of them, plots the estimates in order and, in their proposal, tests the curve as a whole against a null distribution built by permutation, that is, by reshuffling the data so that any true effect is removed. The [Multiverse page](../results.qmd) uses this form of display. A distinct strand kept the data and the question fixed and varied the *analysts* instead: 29 teams answering one question about football referees with odds ratios spanning 0.89 to 2.93 [@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne]; 73 teams testing one hypothesis about immigration and social policy, with more than 95% of the variance in their results left unexplained even after coding every identifiable decision in the workflow of every team [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]; and the Multi100 project, which put at least five independent reanalysts on one claim from each of 100 published studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The EU-frames case you worked on is one of those hundred, and the five analysts whose results the [case page](../case/index.qmd#sec-reanalysts) presents are its reanalysts. A further strand proposes Bayesian hierarchical modelling as the way to aggregate such team-science data, extended into a multiverse over inclusion criteria and priors [@HoogeveenEtAl2020ImprovingStatisticalAnalysis]. The course design combines these strands: the curve of the claim is a model multiverse, the five Multi100 analysts and your own class chart are a many-analysts layer beside it, and the two are meant to be read against each other.

## 2. Three purposes {#sec-purposes}

Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask the organising question of the current debate, which is what a multiverse is actually *for*. Their answer distinguishes three purposes – "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1] – and attaches a characteristic failure to each: "it fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis", and "it fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1]. Their conclusion is mild. The multiverse "does remain a valuable tool", but they "urge against taking it too seriously" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1].

The taxonomy matters most for how a multiverse is built, because the three purposes impose *incompatible* building rules on the universe of specifications. A multiverse built for critique may legitimately mix analyses that answer slightly different questions, because the aim is to document that researchers plausibly disagree about the question – "it may be perfectly sensible to include analyses with different estimands as long as it is plausible that researchers may try out different estimands" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The same set then cannot be read as inference about one quantity, because it no longer targets one quantity. Hullman states the condition in a companion blog post: "what kinds of equivalence are needed will also depend on your goal in using a multiverse" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood]. On this argument, a multiverse can be judged correctly built only relative to the purpose that it is meant to serve.

The course builds its artefacts to different rules for that reason. The fourteen-decision [specification menu](../exercise/spec-menu.qmd), the decision map, the fork chart and the class chart serve reflection in the sense of Rohrer and colleagues, since they exist to make visible how much of a result depends on decisions that look arbitrary from outside, and they show options that answer other questions beside the ones that answer the claim. The curve of `r nrow(curve)` specifications on the [Multiverse page](../results.qmd) is read as evidence about the claim, and it is therefore held to the inferential standard: every specification on it is meant to answer the claim as the course reads it, a claim about change within countries over time in the member states of 2004–2013, and the one decision that leaves two estimands on it, the estimator, is named as such (section 5). Section 3 describes how the course pruned its own menu to meet that standard. The curve-level test designed in the inference reading belongs to the inference purpose as well and inherits the same requirement. If you can say which purpose each artefact of the course serves and which building rule that purpose imposes, you can read the rest of this module, and the papers it cites, as a participant in the argument.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Take the three purposes and assign each artefact of the workshop day to one of them: the specification menu, the preregistration block of your report, the curve of `r nrow(curve)`, the fork chart, the class chart, the permutation test designed in the inference reading. For each assignment, write one sentence on what the universe of specifications would have to look like for that purpose to be legitimately served. Note where one set of analyses is being used for two different purposes.
:::

## 3. The pruning critique {#sec-auspurg}

The most direct empirical disagreement in the recent literature is between Ganslmeier and Vlandas's model-uncertainty study and Katrin Auspurg's reply to it. Ganslmeier and Vlandas cross five specification dimensions at once – control set, fixed-effect structure, standard-error type, sample, and outcome operationalisation – across four political-science literatures, producing roughly 3.6 billion estimates, and find that "the sign and statistical significance of estimates is more contingent on the underlying sample and the operationalization of indicators than on the inclusion of the control set" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6]. They are alert to the obvious objection, stating the dilemma themselves: "Running all possible models risks introducing errors in the empirical approach, but selecting a subset of robustness checks risks reintroducing the 'researcher's degree of freedom'" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 2].

The title of Auspurg's reply promises that robustness is better assessed with a few thoughtful models than with billions of regressions, but the paper itself argues for a narrower precondition, that "Multiverse analyses are only informative when all included models represent equally plausible strategies for estimating the same estimand" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Her charge is that the set is *heterogeneous*, in statistical quality and in what each model estimates, so that its distribution pools numbers that cannot meaningfully be compared with one another. She names four kinds of nonequivalence: statistically inferior models ("Many models do not include fixed effects or cluster-robust SE, which are standard in panel data analyses" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]); unstable country subsets; causal misspecification from randomly combined covariates; and measurement nonequivalence, where "Outcomes differ in scope … and are sometimes negatively correlated. This clearly indicates that they do not reflect the same construct" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Restricting Ganslmeier and Vlandas's universe to models she classes as justified (1,152 of them, against 91,008 unjustified) turns a 60/40 split among significant coefficients into 97% pointing the same way. She also rules out filtering by model fit, noting that "Ironically, the authors' own fit criterion (AIC) consistently favors unjustified models" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. The remedy therefore comes before estimation, in what she calls "thorough, theory-based model selection" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 2].

The constructive version of the same demand is in Young and Cumberworth's book – the current how-to manual for the method, and worth reading whole if this module interests you [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational]. Their rule is **estimand consistency**: "When an estimand is defined a priori by a set of controls, the multiverse model set must always include those controls" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 56], and "any 'necessary control' requires a clear causal diagram or definitional justification supported by prior research" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 57]. The last clause describes the order of the workshop day, where the DAG in Part 2 comes before the preregistration of Task 5 in Part 4. Their book is about *robustness*, and they are explicit that robustness does not identify the true effect: "there is nothing in the distribution of estimates per se that tells us which is the true effect" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 119]. The analyst still owes the reader a defended preferred estimate.

The course applied her test, and the stricter standard that Rohrer and colleagues set for a multiverse used for inference, to its own menu. Every option of every decision was asked one question, whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim as the course reads it, and the options that failed left the curve without leaving the course. Three of her categories reappeared. The pooled estimator, fitted without country effects, falls in her first category, and so do the conventional standard errors of the fixed-effects designs, which treat the ten years of a country as independent although the residuals of a country correlate from one year to the next; the curve keeps the two fixed-effects designs and classes every point by a wild cluster bootstrap by country, as the [statistical methods module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) explains. The four restricted samples, two periods and two sets of excluded countries, are versions of her second category, and the findings that they carry moved to the displays of section 8. Her fourth category, measurement nonequivalence, described the outcome axis of the full menu, on which six framing scales of different scope stood in for 'EU framing'.

The six scales are shares of one instrument that sum to one for each respondent, so whatever raises one must lower the others, and [the simulation module](simulation.qmd#sec-outcomes) lets you examine the arithmetic directly. Under the convention of the course panel, which scores a respondent who mentions nothing as zero, the cell means of the positive and the negative composites sum to one minus the share of silent respondents, so that a confirmation of the claim on the negative composite largely counts the result on the positive composite a second time. The communitarian scale also contains the item "unemployment", which ties the outcome to the predictor by content. The curve of the claim therefore keeps the three positive scales that the claim names, scored as shares, as the paper scores them, while the negative scales have a curve of their own as the other half of the first hypothesis of the paper, and the count of items, which measures how much a respondent says about the EU rather than how the EU is framed, is taught in the [items module](measurement.qmd).

@fig-off-curve shows what each option that left the curve does when it is swapped into every specification of the curve with everything else held as it was. The reason recorded for each, in the list of options that the specification menu draws on (`data/menu_options.csv`), is one of three: the option answers another question, it answers this question less well because an assumption that it needs fails on these data, or it is a check of an answer that the curve already holds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-off-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Options that left the curve of the claim, each swapped into the specifications of the curve to which it applies: the share of the refitted specifications that lie below zero with p < 0.05. The vertical line marks the curve itself (", pct(below_sig(curve)), "). Each option is tested under the rule that fits it: the wild cluster bootstrap for linear models fitted by least squares, errors clustered by country on 26 degrees of freedom for random effects, the beta family and the imputed variants, and CR2 for the within–between model. The two imputation engines cover 24 specifications; the count stands for the rate, whose t and partial correlation are identical. Sources: `data/menu_deviations.csv`, `data/menu_options.csv`.")'
judgement_label <- c(other_question = "answers another question",
                     weaker_answer = "answers this question less well",
                     check = "a check of an answer on the curve")
rule_kept <- c("wcr_rademacher", "re_cr1_g1", "rewb_cr2", "beta_cr1_g1", "mi_rubin_cr1_g1")
off <- devs |>
  filter(!on_curve, axis != "se", option != "rate", rule %in% rule_kept) |>
  left_join(menu |> select(axis, option, label, judgement), by = c("axis", "option")) |>
  mutate(judgement = factor(judgement_label[judgement], judgement_label),
         label = reorder(label, below_zero_sig))
ggplot(off, aes(below_zero_sig, label, colour = judgement)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = below_sig(curve), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = below_zero_sig, yend = label), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0e3b6a", "#0f6b6b", "#8c5a10"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "below zero with p < 0.05", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Read against Auspurg, the pruning changes the picture in the direction that her reply to Ganslmeier and Vlandas leads one to expect. Of the specifications on the curve, `r pct(below(curve))` lie below zero and `r pct(below_sig(curve))` lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05. The options that answer other questions pull the share down furthest, pooled OLS to `r pct(dv("estimator", "pooled_cl", "below_zero_sig"))` and the exclusion of the bailout countries to `r pct(dv("sample", "no_bailout", "below_zero_sig"))`, while the options that answer the same question in another way stay close to the curve, among them the split rule for silent respondents at `r pct(dv("noop", "split", "below_zero_sig"))`. The options that left the curve remain on the menu, the decision map and the class chart as material for reflection, each with its reason attached. That is a disclosure, and disclosure does not supply the justification that Auspurg demands; the justification lies in the reasons, which a reader can contest option by option.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Pick one decision of the [specification menu](../exercise/spec-menu.qmd) and write Auspurg's case for pruning it. Which of her four nonequivalence categories applies, and what would the curve look like if the decision were fixed at its best-justified option? Then write the case for keeping it, in Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's terms: which purpose does varying this decision serve? The estimator and the sample are the two decisions where both cases are strong. Compare what you have written with the reason that the menu gives for each option.
:::

## 4. The one-correct-analysis position {#sec-lakens}

Lakens, Rasti and Tunç push the criticism one level deeper than Auspurg. Their target is the inference that many people draw from analytic variability, namely that since reasonable analyses disagree, there is no single correct analysis, and researchers should report distributions instead of settling on one analysis. Their reply depends on the distinction between two kinds of uncertainty, which they insist must not be merged. *Aleatoric* uncertainty is random variation, the kind that statistics quantifies with standard errors. *Epistemic* uncertainty is uncertainty about which auxiliary assumptions are true – which measure is valid, which units belong in the sample, which adjustment set closes the back-doors. On their view, epistemic uncertainty is reduced by doing research, and widening intervals only absorbs it. Once the auxiliary assumptions are fixed, "there is a fact of the matter about which analysis correctly implements that test" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 7], which is the claim that gives the paper its title. Robustness across specifications of unequal justification counts for nothing, because robustness "is a consequence of valid tests, and not a goal in itself" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 15]. One of their warnings applies directly to teaching exercises: "Variability across specifications based on uninformed hunches, especially when less plausible alternatives are included, provides little actionable insight" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 10].

The pruning described in section 3 moves some way towards their position. The inference rule of the curve, for instance, was decided from evidence about the data, the correlation of the residuals of a country from year to year and the few countries that carry most of the variation, rather than from convention, which is the kind of empirical work on an auxiliary assumption that they ask for. It stops short of their position on the estimator, where the curve keeps two designs because the claim, as written, does not say whether the changes common to all of Europe belong to the comparison, and their argument would require the analyst to settle that question before the test.

It is tempting to answer them with Task 5 of the course, where you fixed a single specification in your preregistration before running it, since that sounds like their prescription. The two devices, however, solve different problems. Preregistration solves a *timing* problem: it rules out choosing the specification once you have seen where the numbers fall, and that answers a genuine worry. Rohrer and colleagues note that "in the absence of preregistration, researchers may as well determine what is equivalent based on whether or not it supports their result" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 5]. The argument of Lakens and colleagues is about *warrant*, which does not depend on timing, since an arbitrary choice remains arbitrary when it is preregistered. It demands the groundwork that makes a choice non-arbitrary – validated measures, established adjustment sets, empirical evidence about the auxiliary assumptions – and the course moves in that direction only through the estimand and DAG work of Part 2, which introduces that groundwork without completing it. A participant choosing one specification from a fourteen-decision menu after ninety minutes of instruction is, on their reading, still choosing on an uninformed hunch. That limits what the exercise demonstrates without invalidating it.

Two further caveats belong here, both cutting against the device that the course itself uses. Preregistering a reanalysis of data you have already seen is itself a compromised form of it, since "[w]hen the data already exist, authors can explore the data prior to registering their analysis – making it unclear what if anything was truly preregistered" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 149]. That is why the course points you to the secondary-data template in [the repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-prereg-templates), which is designed for data that already exist. The two devices can also be combined: "one could preregister a multiverse analysis to combine the strengths of both approaches" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. Preregistering the whole universe of specifications, and only then running it, is the strongest available reply to the charge that multiverse analysis launders analytic flexibility.

## 5. The fork chart {#sec-forks}

The fork chart of the course decomposes the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation across the `r nrow(curve)` specifications of the curve by decision. The estimator carries `r pct(fk("estimator"))`, the predictor `r pct(fk("predictor"))`, the choice among the three positive scales `r pct(fk("outcome"))` and the adjustment set `r pct(fk("copredictor"))`, while the decisions of measurement together carry a few per cent and the interactions between decisions `r pct(fk("interactions"))`. Moving the estimator alone changes whether a specification lies below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 in `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, and moving the predictor alone in `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))`. Numbers like these invite a particular over-claim when they are put to the critics.

The over-claim would be that the dispersion on the curve is estimator dispersion rather than estimand dispersion, so that Auspurg's diagnosis no longer applies. The critics would reply that the estimator fork *is* an estimand fork in their sense, and on this curve the course agrees with them. Both designs that remain compare a country with itself over time, but the two-way design does so relative to the common European path of each year, while the design with country effects alone keeps the changes that every member state went through together, so that the two answer related but different questions, as the [statistical methods module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-two-designs) explains. The curve keeps both because both are defensible readings of the claim, and it names them as two estimands rather than presenting their spread as uncertainty about one quantity. The predictor is a fork of the same kind, since unemployment and GDP growth are two measures of 'poor national economic performance' between which the claim does not choose.

The decomposition supports a more modest reading, in which it *locates* where the argument has to happen. That use is endorsed by every party to the debate. Lakens and colleagues "support the use of multimodel analyses to hypothesize about 'which analytical decisions are most consequential'" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 6]; Ganslmeier and Vlandas offer their method as something that "can help inform which combinations of choices are more or less warranted" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6]; Steegen and colleagues promised pointers to the most consequential choices from the start. Read this way, the fork chart identifies which decisions of the menu need a theory. A large estimator share means that you have to decide whether your question concerns change relative to the common European path or all change within a country, and a large predictor share means that you have to decide which measure of the economy the claim is about.

## 6. Frequency and probability {#sec-reading}

One practical rule from the critical literature concerns how to *read* a specification curve, and it takes the form of a prohibition on treating frequency as probability. The share of specifications supporting a claim – `r pct(below(curve))` below zero on the curve of `r nrow(curve)`, `r pct(below_sig(curve))` below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 – is a description of a curated set of analyses, not the probability that the claim is true. Reading it as a vote invites what Rohrer and colleagues call an illusion. Their prescription is that "variation should be treated possibilistically", meaning that any result occurring anywhere in a justified universe is a live possibility, and that reading has its own condition: "This possibilistic interpretation is only sensible if every universe included is indeed deemed justified" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The Milliways project makes the same point operationally, showing how standard displays emphasise how *often* an outcome occurs and thereby invite "misleading, probabilistic conclusions" [@SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses]. Lakens and colleagues state the bluntest version: "Scientists should not compute the percentage of agreement across different data-analytic strategies, because we do not resolve scientific disagreement by majority vote" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 16].

When the course quotes these shares, they describe the curve that you are looking at, and the [inference reading](../exercise/reading-inference.qmd) exists to police the boundary between that description and any claim about evidence. For the permutation test designed in that reading, this means that a probabilistic device, the permutation p-value, is applied to an object that the current literature says should be read possibilistically. The reading explains what the test licenses under its sharp null, the hypothesis that the effect is zero in every unit, and this module adds a warning about everything that the test does not license.

Rohrer and colleagues also observe that a multiverse persuades only under a precondition: "This can only work if the results are fairly unambiguous across specifications" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 3]. On the curve of the claim the direction of the association meets that precondition, but the strength of the evidence does not, since whether a specification clears the 5% threshold depends mainly on the estimator: `r pct(below_sig(country))` of the specifications with country effects alone lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct(below_sig(twoway))` of the two-way ones, and the reproduced specification itself has a bootstrap p-value of `r num(ref$p_wcr)`. The curve can therefore persuade a reader that the association runs in the direction of the claim within countries, and it leaves open whether the evidence is strong once the changes common to all of Europe are removed, which is a question about the estimand as much as about the data. The threshold itself carries its usual meaning here, because the bootstrap tests each specification against the variation of the countries, whose CR2 degrees of freedom (a median of `r num(median(curve$df_cr2), 1)` across the curve) suggest that about a dozen of them effectively carry the information, rather than against the hundreds of thousands of respondents that make almost any coefficient significant in a respondent-level model. If you ever build a multiverse to defend a result of your own, this is the precondition to check before you lean on it.

On the workshop day it is easy to read the live class chart, on which every submitted specification appears as a dot on one curve, as the persuasive set piece of the day. The critical literature describes it better as a **many-analysts demonstration**, the classroom analogue of the 29 teams and the 73 teams, with the extra property that every declared specification, drawn as a filled circle, was fixed in the Task 5 preregistration before it was run, while the specifications that were tried with `try_spec()` and submitted with `submit_exploration()` in Task 4 are drawn as open circles. Heyman and Vanpaemel, who run multiverse projects with students, describe the design as "comparable to the many-analysts-one-dataset approach used by Silberzahn et al. (2018)" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 7], and note that when several analysts each make their own analytical choices, "there is a multiverse of multiverse analyses" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 7]. Disagreement among the analysts in a class is no verdict on robustness in either direction, but it demonstrates that the dispersion documented by the many-analysts literature is real, reproducible and, once the menu and the preregistrations are on the table, *explainable*. The chart therefore serves reflection, practised as a group, and this is also the answer to anyone who asks why the class chart is allowed to straddle zero.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [the Multiverse page](../results.qmd) and find the filled circle for the specification that you declared in Task 5 (or the reproduced specification, if you did not submit one). First read its neighbourhood possibilistically: what is the full range of aligned estimates among specifications that differ from yours on exactly one decision? Then catch yourself the moment you start counting – 'most of my neighbours agree with me' – and write one sentence on what that count would and would not establish, given how this universe was built.
:::

## 7. The multiverse in the classroom {#sec-teaching}

Every side of this debate agrees that the multiverse is useful in the classroom. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman, in the middle of urging everyone not to take it too seriously, concede without reservation that "the multiverse has been a valuable training tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 8]. Heyman and Vanpaemel build their whole teaching design on it, and the construction of this course follows their two rules of classroom practice. The first puts the motivation for each path before the number of paths, since "the goal should not be to merely devise as many paths as possible" and "[t]he key is that the alternatives are properly motivated" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 4]. That is why the course offers a menu of decisions with a reason attached to every option.

The second rule is pastoral: "one should be cautious that students do not completely lose faith in (psychological) science" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. A day spent following one published claim through hundreds of specifications, and through the options that were set beside them, can leave participants cynical about research, and the day is structured to work against that. The materials of this case that are public on the OSF form a record that anyone can check, and preregistration, practised in Task 5, makes the record of your own future analyses equally checkable. Taught with that caution in mind, the multiverse shows that the decisions behind an analysis can be identified and defended, and that they belong to the analyst who made them.

Hullman gives a further reason why this literacy will matter more in future. Multiverse construction is becoming cheap, because "lots of forms of robustness checking that used to be difficult are now trivially easy" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood] once a generative-AI agent can build the universe from a paper. When anyone can produce a specification curve on demand, the scarce skill lies in judging what belongs in the universe, naming the purpose that it serves, and refusing the readings that its construction cannot support.

## 8. Heterogeneity and influence {#sec-heterogeneity}

The four sample restrictions of the menu left the curve because each changes the population about which the claim is made, but the findings that they carry belong in the course, and three displays keep them. Each answers a question that a curve of one population cannot answer, namely where and when in that population the association is found, and none of them adds a point to the curve.

@fig-periods fits the 36 core specifications of the curve – the three positive scales on raw or logged unemployment or on growth, with or without the other measure of the economy, under both fixed-effects designs – on the full panel and on each half of it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-periods
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The 36 core specifications of the curve on the full panel and on each half of it, by design. Open circles have bootstrap p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the lines join the fits of one specification, and the burgundy line is the reproduced specification and its twin with country effects alone. The vertical axis is the claim-aligned partial correlation, so below zero is the direction of the claim. Source: `data/display_periods.csv`."
per_plot <- periods |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         period = factor(sample, c("all", "y2004_2008", "y2009_2013"),
                         c("2004–2013", "2004–2008", "2009–2013")),
         p_class = if_else(p_wcr < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"),
         spec = paste(outcome, predictor, copredictor, pred_form),
         reproduced = is_ref_spec(periods))
ggplot(per_plot, aes(period, r_ca, group = spec)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = filter(per_plot, reproduced), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = filter(per_plot, reproduced), aes(shape = p_class),
             colour = "#8b1538", size = 2.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = minus) +
  facet_wrap(vars(design)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "claim-aligned partial r") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(per_ref("all", "b"), 5)` on the full panel (bootstrap p = `r num(per_ref("all", "p_wcr"))`), `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "b"), 5)` on 2004–2008 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "p_wcr"), 4)`) and `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "b"), 5)` on 2009–2013 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "p_wcr"))`), so that each half on its own gives a steeper slope than the panel as a whole, and among the 24 unemployment specifications `r pct(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "all")))` lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 on the full panel, `r pct(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2004_2008")))` on 2004–2008 and `r pct(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2009_2013")))` on 2009–2013. Neither half is a second answer to whether framing changed with the crisis. The earlier window contains no crisis, so its slope describes how framing tracked the smaller fluctuations of those years, and the later one drops the comparison with the years before the crisis and asks how framing moved with the deepening and easing of the crisis once it had begun. Read together, the two halves suggest that the association is not confined to the crisis years, and that it is somewhat stronger once the crisis had started.

@fig-loo leaves one country out at a time, from the reproduced specification and from its twin with country effects alone. The variation that identifies the two-way slope is concentrated in a few countries: once the fixed effects are removed, Greece holds `r pct(vs("GR"))` of the variation in unemployment that is left, Spain `r pct(vs("ES"))`, Poland `r pct(vs("PL"))` and Ireland `r pct(vs("IE"))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-loo
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "The slope of the cosmopolitan share on unemployment with one country left out at a time, under each design. Open circles have bootstrap p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the burgundy line marks the slope on all 27 countries. Countries are ordered by the two-way slope without them. Source: `data/display_loo.csv`."
country_order <- loo_two |>
  left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  arrange(desc(b)) |>
  pull(country)
loo_plot <- loo |>
  filter(left_out != "none") |>
  left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         country = factor(country, country_order),
         p_class = if_else(p_wcr < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"))
loo_full <- loo |>
  filter(left_out == "none") |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label))
ggplot(loo_plot, aes(b, country)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(data = loo_full, aes(xintercept = b), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = minus, n.breaks = 4) +
  facet_wrap(vars(design), scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "slope per point of unemployment, without the country", y = "country left out") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Leaving out one country moves the two-way slope between `r num(min(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.min(loo_two$b)]]`) and `r num(max(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.max(loo_two$b)]]`). None of the 27 two-way refits reaches bootstrap p < 0.05, as the full panel does not, while `r sum(loo_cty$p_wcr < 0.05)` of the 27 refits with country effects alone do. The display replaces a single hand-picked exclusion, such as leaving out Greece and Spain together, with the complete set, and its 27 refits are 27 checks of one answer rather than 27 answers.

@tbl-bailout fits the three positive scales on unemployment in the eight countries that received financial assistance and in the other nineteen separately, and tests the difference between the two groups in one model on all 270 cells. With eight clusters the Rademacher bootstrap can draw only 256 distinct sign patterns, so the table reads the Webb signs for the bailout countries.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bailout
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Slopes on unemployment in the eight bailout countries (Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania, Spain), in the other nineteen, and the difference between the two, estimated in one model on all 270 cells with an interaction. Bootstrap p-values in brackets, with Webb signs for the bailout countries and Rademacher signs otherwise. Source: `data/display_bailout.csv`."
bailout |>
  filter(predictor == "unemp") |>
  mutate(p = if_else(group == "bailout", p_wcr_webb, p_wcr),
         cell = paste0(num(b, 5), " (", num(p), ")")) |>
  select(outcome, estimator, group, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = cell) |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, c("mcosmo", "mutil", "mpos")),
         estimator = factor(estimator, names(design_label))) |>
  arrange(outcome, estimator) |>
  transmute(Scale = c(mcosmo = "cosmopolitan", mutil = "utilitarian",
                      mpos = "positive composite")[as.character(outcome)],
            Design = design_label[as.character(estimator)],
            `Bailout countries` = bailout, `Other countries` = other,
            Difference = difference) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = 3:5, align = "r") |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(ba("bailout", "b"), 5)` in the bailout countries (Webb p = `r num(ba("bailout", "p_wcr_webb"))`) and +`r num(ba("other", "b"), 5)` in the others (p = `r num(ba("other", "p_wcr"), 2)`), and the difference of `r num(ba("difference", "b"), 5)` has bootstrap p = `r num(ba("difference", "p_wcr"))`. The pattern holds for the cosmopolitan share and the positive composite under the two-way design, while the utilitarian scale does not share it.

Read together, the three displays suggest that the association between unemployment and positive framing is concentrated in the countries and the years in which the crisis was deepest, which is what a reader of the claim needs to know about it. The reason for keeping them off the curve is the requirement of section 2. A curve that mixed the full panel with its halves and its subsets would count answers about different populations as votes on one question, and its share of supporting specifications would then depend on how many restrictions the menu happened to offer. As displays, the same fits show how the association varies across the population of the claim, which is a finding in its own right, without being read as evidence that the claim is robust or fragile.

The book-length how-to is @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the tooling is @SarmaEtAl2023MultiverseMultiplexingAlternative and @SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses; the classroom design is @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom. Quotations from the two PsyArXiv preprints are cited by the pagination of the preprints themselves. The numbers on this page are computed when it is built from files that the course pipeline writes: the curve `data/spec_curve.csv` and its decomposition `data/spec_curve_forks.csv`, the comparison of every option with its twins on the curve in `data/menu_deviations.csv`, the reasons in `data/menu_options.csv`, and the displays `data/display_periods.csv`, `data/display_loo.csv` and `data/display_bailout.csv`, which the [codebook of the displays](../data/displays_codebook.md) describes.
